analysis.one_liner: Limits how long health insurers can delay coverage for preexisting conditions to three months.
analysis.headline: The bill never reached a floor vote; it sat in three House committees for about 18 months, got one hearing, and died when the Congress ended, despite 46 House sponsors and cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the rules then in force, a health plan could look back six months into your medical history and then refuse to pay for anything it found for up to a year, or 18 months if you enrolled late. This bill would have cut the look-back to 30 days and the exclusion to three months (nine for late enrollees), applied the same limits to individually purchased insurance, and ended a rule requiring people to first use up COBRA continuation coverage before getting guaranteed individual coverage. It never got out of committee.
analysis.who_benefits: People changing jobs, losing a job, or buying their own insurance who had a health condition — cancer, diabetes, pregnancy, a past injury — and would otherwise face months or years of treatment being denied as 'preexisting.' Also people locked out of the individual market because they hadn't exhausted COBRA coverage.

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the look-back window plans can use to identify preexisting conditions from six months to 30 days [S2][S3].
Caps the preexisting condition exclusion at three months (nine for late enrollees), down from 12 to 18 months [S2][S3].
Applies the same group-market limits to individually purchased health insurance, where exclusions were previously less constrained [S2][S3].
Removes the requirement that a person elect and exhaust COBRA continuation coverage before qualifying for guaranteed individual coverage [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, who would lose a tool for keeping costly enrollees' claims off their books for a year or more, and to a small degree other policyholders if insurers spread the added claims cost into premiums.

drawbacks.text: Insurers argued that shorter exclusion periods mean they pay claims for people who enroll already sick, and that those costs get spread into higher premiums for everyone else; the bill's own three-month carve-out for people switching individual plans shows the drafters recognized the risk of people waiting until they are sick to buy coverage [S2][S3].

The bill keeps preexisting condition exclusions legal outright, rather than banning them as later law did, so a person treated for a condition in the past month could still face a three-month gap in coverage for it [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and large for a specific group: people with known conditions who change or lose coverage would get treatment paid for instead of waiting out a year or more of exclusions. The cost — modestly higher premiums spread across all enrollees — is real but diffuse, and the bill's phased effective dates, including a delay for collectively bargained plans, acknowledge the transition burden. On balance this was a targeted consumer protection, though it fell well short of banning the practice entirely.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three different House committees, got one hearing in March 2008, was never voted out of any of them, and died when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Courtney introduced the bill on June 22, 2007, joined by Rep. George Miller of California [S3][S5].

The Speaker referred it to three committees at once — Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, and Ways and Means — a split referral that requires any of them to act before the bill can advance [S5].
It was sent to the Health and the Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions subcommittees [S5].
Committee hearings were held on March 20, 2008, but no committee ever marked up or reported the bill [S5].
The bill attracted 45 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no further action was taken before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers kept the existing rules — a six-month look-back and 12-to-18-month exclusions — for another two-plus years until the Affordable Care Act replaced them with a ban. People with preexisting conditions gained nothing in the meantime.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers; people with preexisting conditions waited

industries.note: The bill would strip insurers of their ability to look back six months and deny payment for up to 18 months for conditions people already had — a tool that shifted the cost of sick people onto the patients themselves and onto anyone else who picked up their care. Insurers would instead bear those claims and spread them into premiums.

Employers would face conforming rule changes for their plans, with a delay of up to three years for collectively bargained plans to soften the transition. Most of the direct burden falls on insurers, not plan sponsors.
